description: Mission Maker is an interactive space game where students become space scientists and design their own missions to explore the Moon, Mars and beyond. Players choose rockets, build spacecraft, select scientific tools and manage limited resources like budget, fuel, power and weight. They then launch and simulate their missions, learning how every decision affects success. The game makes space science fun while developing creativity, problem-solving and decision-making skills.
summary: Mission Control Academy is a kid-friendly game where players design, launch and run a NASA-style mission to Mars, the Moon or Earth. Every choice trades off money, weight, power, data, signal and lifetime. After launch, real NASA photos and space-weather data show what the mission discovered.
details:
The problem. Real space missions are a puzzle of competing limits: a better instrument adds mass, power, cost and data. Students rarely get to try a whole mission from idea to operation, so these trade-offs stay abstract.

Our solution. Mission Control Academy turns mission design into a simple, colorful game for ages 7 and up. A robot guide named Nova explains every step in short sentences. Players pick a destination (Earth, Moon or Mars), a spacecraft size (from CubeSat to large observatory), instruments, power and communications hardware, a rocket and an orbit.

What players see. Six live bars (money, weight, power, data, signal, lifetime) change with every choice. When something doesn’t fit, such as a rocket too small to reach Mars or a ship too heavy to launch, Nova explains why in plain words and offers a fix. Locked options show a “Why is this locked?” reason.

Learning loop. Players compare two alternative designs, verify a Pass/Fail checklist with reasons, then launch. The mission earns a score out of 100 (science value, requirements met, efficient resource use, surviving events, trade-space exploration) and a report that explains what worked, what failed and why, with tips to improve. [confirm: launch phase, events and report match the live game]

Real NASA connection. After a mission, players see real NASA photos of the world they studied in a research gallery. The game’s missions are modeled on real NASA missions: LRO (Moon), MAVEN and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Mars) and Terra and Landsat (Earth). Spacecraft sizes follow NASA’s CubeSat standards.

Play together. The design supports one to four players with NASA-inspired roles (Mission Designer, Spacecraft Engineer, Communications and Ground Officer, Science Lead). [confirm: online rooms working, or say “one-screen team play” and “online rooms in progress”]

Built for everyone. It works on phones and laptops, needs no login, has a sandbox mode, a high-contrast option and a lightweight 2D default. It is built with Next.js, deployed on Vercel, and was created with AI assistance (see section 4).

Impact. The game helps students understand that there is rarely one perfect design, only good trade-offs, which is the heart of real mission engineering.
